13656-a-series-of-lessons-in-raja-yoga:
Yogi Ramacharaka's Series of Lessons in Raja Yoga, first issued monthly from October 1905 to September 1906, gathers twelve lessons in permanent form in 1906. The publishers note a hearty public response, and the author, known for Hatha Yoga, psychic healing, and the science of breath, presents Raja Yoga as the yoga of mind.

A central exercise concentrates on the words I AM, not I am this or that. I do this or think that, but mere being itself, gathering mental energies at the centre of being. Unconscious rumination, where new views rearrange old opinions over days, weeks, or months, shows how mind digests ideas unseen. Ramacharaka writes for students who want mental discipline behind yogic practice.
17682-the-healthy-life-vol-v-nos-24-28-t:
The Healthy Life, the independent health magazine, fills this fifth volume, covering July to December, with numbers twenty-four to twenty-eight. Its transcriber corrected a small number of obvious typographical errors, including two mentioned in the September issue, without marking each in the text. The fuller edition marks them in its web version.

As a half-year's run, the magazine mixes articles on diet, exercise, fresh air, and natural health, in the earnest manner of the health reform press. Readers get a snapshot of early twentieth-century health fads and sound advice side by side. The volume suits readers of health history and of periodical culture.
17919-the-story-of-burnt-njal-from-the-i:
Sir George Webbe Dasent turned the Njals Saga into English as The Story of Burnt Njal. It was printed in New York and London in 1900, with a preface and a cut-down introduction from the 1861 edition. Dasent, a famed Victorian translator of Norse tales, gives the saga its classic English form.

The tale runs from Fiddle Mord and Hrut's wooing to Gunnar's stand at home, where he cries that fair is Lithe and he will not fare abroad. Feuds, law, fire, and fate drive the long story to its grim end. It is one of the great sagas, stern, noble, and tragic, and Dasent's version keeps its grave, old music.
17946-eirik-the-red-s-saga:
The Reverend J. Sephton translated Eirik the Red's Saga and read it before the Literary and Philosophical Society of Liverpool on January 12, 1880. The Liverpool firm D. Marples printed the short book the same year.

The saga tells how Vifil came to Iceland, how Eirik found Greenland, and how Leif, his son, found Vinland across the sea. Gudrid's marriages, Karlsefni's voyage, and fights with the Skraelings fill the later chapters. Sephton's version is plain and faithful, a short, clear door into the Norse voyages to the New World, and a tale of bold sailors, stern winters, and new shores.
19929-cad-metti-the-female-detective-str:
Cad Metti, the Female Detective Strategist, is a dime novel of the 1890s. Its enemy is a gang called the worst ever known. Italians lead it, with American and English rogues in contingent. They are the most dangerous operators ever organized for coining. Counterfeit money is their trade, and Cad Metti hunts them. Her opponent Dudie Dunne shares the title page. Edward L. Wheeler's school of dime fiction runs on such stakes.

Female detectives were a daring novelty in dime novels. Cad Metti outwits criminals and male rivals alike. The counterfeiting plot taps a real federal obsession. Secret Service men hunted coiners across the era. Wheeler-style sensation kept facts at arm's length. The tale preserves pulp crime in its rawest form.
20113-nonsense-drolleries-the-owl-the-pu:
Nonsense Drolleries gathers Edward Lear's famed nonsense verse, with pictures by William Foster. The Owl and the Pussy-Cat sail away for a year and a day. They land where the Bong-tree grows, in Lear's bright, odd world. There a Piggy-wig stands in a wood with a ring in his nose.

That ring solves the pair's search for a wedding band at last. Lear's rhymes mix sweet tunes with words that mean nothing at all. Generations of children have loved that mix of sense and fun. The book keeps his best loved nonsense songs in one handy place.
23662-the-heart-of-unaga:
Ridgwell Cullum published this northern adventure novel in 1920, set among the forests, rivers, and winter trails of the far north. Its first part follows Julyman's tales of the Sleeper Indians and the going of Steve. It also follows the arrival of Marcel Brand and An-ina, with reindeer, a big chief named Wanak-Aha, and a rush outfit bound for remote country.

Fourteen years pass. The second part returns to the same wilderness through new eyes: manhood, a duel, the king of the forest, and the faith of men tested by the season's close. Cullum, a veteran writer of frontier romance, gives readers a long, roaming story of loyalty, love, and survival where the land itself is the strongest character.
26723-a-little-maid-of-ticonderoga:
Alice Turner Curtis published this girls' historical story with the Penn Publishing Company at Philadelphia, copyrighted in 1917 and issued in 1929, illustrated by Wuanita Smith. It joins her Little Maid series, from Province Town and Massachusetts Colony to Bunker Hill, Old Connecticut, Old Philadelphia, and Old Maine. The frontispiece declares, My Name Is Ethan Allen.

Faith Carew is ten when Esther Eldridge comes to visit her log cabin on a Green Mountains hillside, below her father's mill. Faith listens each morning for the mill-stream's gay little song and hopes Esther, a village child, will love the wilderness, its paths, trees, and flowers. Chapters run from Faith's promise and mischief through Kashaqua, the journey, new friends, Louise, secrets, and Louise's disappearance to Faith visiting the fort again and the capture of the fort.
29045-from-the-st-lawrence-to-the-yser-w:
Frederic C. Curry, late captain of the Second Eastern Ontario Regiment, wrote this war book, From the St. Lawrence to the Yser, with the First Canadian Brigade, published in Toronto in 1916. Curry dedicates it to Lieutenant-General Sir Sam Hughes, minister of militia, whose efforts made the Canadian contingents efficient. His chapters run from ante-bellum days and Petewawa through mobilisation, Valcartier, and the convoy to England.

Later chapters follow Ypres in 1915, Festubert, Givenchy, and Messines, with mine warfare, myths and fairies, and the winter months. Pictures show the regiment near Stonehenge, manoeuvres on Salisbury Plain, and trenches at Givenchy. Readers get a Canadian officer's firsthand account of the Great War's first years, from home training to the Yser front.
29608-personal-recollections-of-a-cavalr:
J. H. Kidd, formerly colonel of the Sixth Michigan Cavalry and brevet brigadier general of volunteers, wrote these personal recollections of a cavalryman with Custer's Michigan Cavalry Brigade in the Civil War. Printed at Ionia, Michigan, in 1908 by the Sentinel Printing Company, the book is dedicated to Kidd's wife and son and to his comrades of the brigade.

Kidd draws on official records and on the memoirs of Sheridan and McClellan's cavalry campaigns, giving both sides of the picture where he can. Men reported missing in action, with no further record, receive special care. Readers of Civil War history will find a first-hand, soldierly memoir of Michigan horse soldiers under Custer.
3051-an-open-eyed-conspiracy-an-idyl-of-:
William Dean Howells wrote An Open-Eyed Conspiracy as an idyl of Saratoga, published in Edinburgh by David Douglas in 1898. The story opens on a very hot day under tall trees that embower and stifle Saratoga, shutting out air as well as sun. After tea, the last meal at Saratoga hotels, the narrator strolls to Congress Park for coolness while Mrs. March stays on the hotel verandah.

The idyl follows the Marches and the Deerings, a couple with money who do not know how to buy a good time, and a girl whose presence awes her elders. Howells's comedy of manners turns on American leisure, marriage, and the gap between wealth and ease. The novella remains a charming minor Howells, light in tone and sharp in observation.
30952-with-ethan-allen-at-ticonderoga:
W. Bert Foster wrote this boys' adventure book for the Penn Publishing Company in Philadelphia, with a 1903 copyright and a 1904 printing, and pictures by F. A. Carter. Foster had already written With Washington at Valley Forge. This volume follows young Enoch Harding through the wilderness world that leads to Ethan Allen and Fort Ticonderoga, in twenty-four chapters.

Early chapters give a boy of the wilderness, Enoch feeling himself a man, an ambush, a stratagem, a pioneer home, and a stump burning. A night attack and a traitor's way follow. Later chapters bring the Otter Creek raid, the Westminster Massacre, the rising of the clans, and the escape of a spy. At last comes the dawn of the tenth of May, when the guns of old Ti speak. It is a stirring tale of the Revolution's frontier days.
31388-mother-truth-s-melodies-common-sen:
Mrs. E. P. Miller's Mother Truth's Melodies, a kindergarten of common sense for children, appeared in a new and enlarged edition from Cram in Chicago and Boston in 1896, with four hundred and fifty illustrations. Miller argues little ones are geese no more but knowing, so Mother Truth should replace Mother Goose in the home. She lifts her voice in melodies for babes that parents and children will welcome.

The author insists her pieces are not poetry but simple rhymes, whose jingle may be music in children's ears while their truths leave an impress. They fill young minds so falsehood and false ideas find no room. Suggested by the philanthropist Elizabeth Thompson, the book puts facts in memorable form for the nursery, a Victorian attempt to teach truth through rhyme.
33999-the-bondman-a-new-saga:
Hall Caine wrote this saga, published in New York by A. L. Burt and dedicated to his son Little Sunlocks. Caine sets the central date in 1800, the year Iceland and Ireland both lost their last visible signs of ancient independence. He warns that he has not bound himself to strict chronology, Manx or Icelandic, for years before and after.

Caine draws on Icelandic and English books, and on help from Jon A. Hjaltalin of Modruvellir, to picture old habits, customs, and laws. A foolish revolt at Reykjavik gains the dignity of a serious revolution in his telling. The novel offers a saga of simple passions against a nation's fate.
3425-samantha-at-saratoga:
Marietta Holley sends her comic heroine Samantha Allen to Saratoga Springs in this humorous novel. Samantha, who first appeared as Josiah Allen's wife, speaks in a plain, shrewd voice about fashion, money, and manners at the famous resort. She is not fooled by fine clothes, and she sorts visitors into tramps with broken hats and tramps with diamond earrings and Saratoga trunks.

The humor comes from Samantha's common sense applied to high society. She watches balls, hotels, and shopping with the eye of a farm wife who knows the price of things. Holley, a popular author and suffrage supporter, uses the comedy to defend women's judgment. The book suits readers who enjoy gentle satire and a strong, funny narrator.
347-the-saga-of-grettir-the-strong-grett:
An unknown Icelandic writer of the early fourteenth century tells the life of Grettir, a strong and unlucky outlaw, in this long saga. The tale opens with his kin, viking raids, and the wars that shaped Norway, then follows Grettir from a hard youth to years on the run. Iceland, its farms, and its feuds form the hard ground of the story.

Grettir fights trolls, bears, and men, yet his temper and bad luck keep him outside the law. Friends shelter him; foes hunt him across lonely isles and coasts. The saga mixes grim fights with dry wit, and it ends as a stark portrait of a man too strong for his own good.
35080-a-hero-of-ticonderoga:
A Hero of Ticonderoga is a frontier tale by Rowland Robinson. The book came out in Vermont in the year eighteen ninety eight. Its scene is the wild edge of settlement in the years of revolt. Grants, fort claims, and York men crowd the back tale of the plot.

Seventeen chapters run from a new home in the woods to the fort fight. A bear trap, a sad death, a flight, and free wild life mark the road. Forebodings of storm build as great names take the lead of the bands. The fall of the fort forms the crest of the tale near its end. A home come back in peace caps the arc of the young hero.
40871-fifty-two-stories-of-the-british-n:
Fifty-two Stories of the British Navy, from Damme to Trafalgar, edited by Alfred H Miles, came out in London in its seventh thousand. A front plate shows Nelson taking the swords of Spanish officers on board the San Joseph. Miles dates his note September 1, 1896.

The tales run in time order, as fifty-two links in a chain of a thousand years of sea rule. Miles draws on Campbell and his lives of the admirals, and on Southey and his life of Nelson. He takes the tale of the Revenge near word for word from Sir Walter Raleigh. The Armada comes from Creasy, and Drake and Hawkins get tales of their own. Boys and girls get sea deeds from the Cinque Ports to Trafalgar, told by the best hands.
4278-an-introduction-to-yoga:
Annie Besant, president of the Theosophical Society, gave these four lectures at Benares in December 1907. They were published in 1908. She presents yoga as a science of consciousness. Her topics include the meaning of the universe and the unfolding of the self. They include states of mind and samadhi, the state of absorbed union.

The lectures move from schools of Indian thought and the mental body to yoga as practice. They cover methods, meditation with and without seed, and mantras. They cover attention, obstacles, and purification. Besant writes for listeners new to the subject but serious about it, explaining terms as she goes.
48034-old-broadbrim-into-the-heart-of-au:
Old Broadbrim Into the Heart of Australia is number 32 of the Old Broadbrim Weekly, a five cent detective library from Street and Smith of New York. This number is dated May 9, 1903. The subtitle adds the hook: A Strange Bargain and its Consequences. The writer is named only as the author of Old Broadbrim.

The cover picture shows the climax in advance: a brigand chief orders his men to riddle a prisoner, and the detective's rifle speaks first. The contents run to 19 chapters. A strange bargain and a midnight murder open the case. The trail runs through London before it is spotted in Australia. A terrible death-trap, Demona the ranch queen, and the doom of waters fill the middle. Old Broadbrim makes his catch in Perth before the end. Dime novel readers got the Quaker detective on his longest trail.
48251-the-boy-scouts-down-in-dixie-or-th:
Herbert Carter wrote The Boy Scouts Down in Dixie, or the Strange Secret of Alligator Swamp, copyrighted in 1914 by the Burt Company. Carter's other scout tales fill a list at the front, from the Battle of Saratoga to the Rockies. A line from page 119 stands as the motto: back water, fellows.

Twenty-eight chapters take the khaki boys into the sunny Southland. The early ones teach camp fare and woods lore among puzzling swamp water trails, with Bumpus on guard and a night prowler at the edge of camp. Alligator Smith, the guide, joins at chapter 11. Then come the sheriff's round-up posse, a man-trap, and an oasis in the quaking bog. The mystery is solved in the last chapter, as the title promises. Boy readers of 1914 got the deep swamp without leaving their chairs.
48459-the-motor-boat-club-in-florida-or-:
The Motor Boat Club in Florida, or Laying the Ghost of Alligator Swamp, is a boys' adventure novel by Hancock. It was published at Philadelphia by Henry Altemus, with copyright in 1909. Hancock wrote a whole series of Motor Boat Club books, set on coasts and rivers across the country.

The club cruises south in December weather warm enough to feel like summer. Chapters promise a kink in the Gulf Stream, a haunted swamp, and an island said to hold no alligators. Tom Halstead leads the boys through night alarms and a hunt for the ghost. Later chapters bring a chase in the wake of a boat called the Buzzard, and a fearful two minutes inside a ring of alligators. The tale ends with the ghost laid and the game bagged.
50493-the-black-eagle-or-ticonderoga:
James, author of The Gypsy, Richelieu, and Darnley, wrote The Black Eagle, or Ticonderoga, a historical novel here in a new edition from Routledge of London and New York, 1859. The title joins a chief's name to the great fort on Lake Champlain.

Nearly 40 chapters fill the contents. The two young Prevosts and Edith carry the settler side. A figure called the Woodchuck teaches how to walk the woods. The Brown Maiden and Otaitsa stand on the other side of the forest war. Indian revenge, councils, a fire, and a capture build the middle. Walter disappears and lies in prison. Edith resolves, journeys, and offers self-sacrifice. Readers of frontier romance get the Champlain border in James's stately style.
57723-the-orkneyinga-saga:
Hjaltalin and Goudie translated the Orkneyinga Saga from the Icelandic for Edmonston and Douglas in 1873. Anderson, keeper of the National Museum, edited it with notes and an introduction. A view of Saint Magnus Cathedral fronts the book. The saga is the history of the Orkneymen, earls and odallers of Norse stock who established an earldom in the Scottish isles a thousand years ago.

It begins with the conquest of the isles by Harald Harfagri and follows the line of Norse jarls for three centuries and a half. For that span it is the authority for the history of northern Scotland. The narrative is personal and picturesque, the preface says, recording deeds and what was thought of them at the time. The words of skalds are woven through it, for all history, Anderson argues, has begun in song. Victorian Scotland here recovered its Viking centuries in its own tongue.
59689-the-frithiof-saga:
George P Upton translated a German retelling by Ferdinand Schmidt of the Frithiof saga for young people, published at Chicago in 1907 with four illustrations. Upton's preface calls Iceland the home of the saga form. A saga tells a hero's life in fixed form, usually for recitation, but not in verse. Many sagas survive from Iceland, Greenland, and the Norse lands.

Frithiof is fearless in battle and at sea in his dragon ship, swift to punish and quick to forgive. He loves Ingeborg, King Bele's daughter, but her brothers refuse the match since he is not royal born. She is married to old King Ring, and Frithiof is exiled.
62977-the-civil-war-battles-of-chickamau:
The Civil War Battles of Chickamauga and Chattanooga is a battlefield guide by J L Rogers, in its third edition, sold for fifty cents. Its front cover shows the New York Peace Monument in Point Park on Lookout Mountain. The monument is described as the largest and most imposing structure in the park, at ninety-five feet high.

Its base is fifty feet across, reached by seven steps of Tennessee marble. At the centre of a colonnade a tall shaft rises, crowned by bronze figures of a Union and a Confederate soldier with the flag towering above them. Their hands, once raised in strife, now clasp a brother's hand. The monument was erected in 1907 at a cost of about eighty thousand dollars and dedicated in November 1910. General Sickles, who suggested the design, took great pride in it.
64029-life-at-the-zoo-notes-and-traditio:
Charles Cornish wrote Life at the Zoo, notes and traditions of the Regent's Park Gardens, issued at London in 1895 with photographs by Gambier Bolton. More than forty short chapters range over the whole life of the zoo, from the zoo in a frost to a year at the zoo. Cornish writes of the lion house, diving birds, talking birds, bears, monkeys great and small, and lizards and crocodiles.

Other chapters ask how animals see beauty, scent, sound, and music, and one takes the animals' own point of view. The quest for the wild horse, Jamrach the dealer, and the Paris gardens in two sieges widen the scope past London. It is a warm, close watch of a famed Victorian zoo.
65127-menace-from-vega:
Menace From Vega is a science fiction story by Robert Randall, taken from Imagination magazine for June 1958. The opening question asks why strangers would abduct a girl from a psychiatric ward. Psychiatrist James Lawrence faces a tall, handsome stranger pointing an odd-looking gun at him. The man demands to know about his patient Bette Bauer.

Bette Bauer had once been a brilliant physicist who showed signs of real genius. Something happened to her soon after her doctor's degree in theoretical physics. She has spent three years in St Paul's Neuropsychiatric Hospital, a catatonic patient out of touch with the real world. Lawrence finds, oddly, that facing the gun brings tense expectancy rather than fear. The stranger calls his silence childish and presses on. To answer why such men want Bette, Lawrence must face the threat of the title, from Vega.
73305-voyages-of-the-dutch-brig-of-war-d:
Kolff, a first class lieutenant in the Dutch navy, kept the log of a brig of war called the Dourga on two voyages in 1825 and 1826. George Windsor Earl turned the Dutch text into English, and it came out in London in 1840. The brig sailed through the little known south parts of the Moluccas and along the unknown south coast of New Guinea.

Kolff calls his tale plain and unadorned, the work of a seaman and not a man of letters. Friends in India and at home urged him to print what he saw, for the use of state men, sea officers, and plain readers. Hard years at sea, plus the Celebes campaign of 1824, had worn his health down.
8518-fritiofs-saga:
Esaias Tegnér's Fritiofs Saga appears here in an edition for American students, with introduction, bibliography, notes, and vocabulary edited by Andrew A. Stomberg. The preface explains that courses in Swedish in a few American colleges created a need for Swedish texts with vocabularies and notes. The model of German texts, and this volume meets it.

Tegnér's saga retells the Norse tale of Frithiof, hero, lover, and exile, in verse that made it Sweden's most popular poem. Stomberg's edition suits students learning Swedish through literature, with help on every page. Readers get both a classic of Swedish romanticism and a language textbook, in one volume.
a-series-of-lessons-in-raja-yoga: William Walker Atkinson offers lessons in Raja Yoga, first issued as monthly lessons from October 1905 to September 1906 and then gathered unchanged into this volume. The publishers note the hearty public response that called for a permanent form, and the amount of information condensed into each lesson. Students, they report, found each lesson needed careful reading and study, a discipline of mind rather than a book to be hurried.
an-introduction-to-yoga:
An Introduction to Yoga is a set of lectures by Annie Besant, first given for readers new to the subject. Besant was a British socialist, theosophist, and women's rights campaigner, and a famous orator who also supported Irish and Indian self-rule. In these lectures she turns teacher, setting out to give an outline of yoga in plain order.

The lectures introduce yoga as a path of disciplined inner development, presented through the theosophical frame Besant taught. They aim to orient a beginner: what yoga is, what it demands, and how its practice is organized. The book remains a clear period document of how yoga was first explained to English-speaking audiences in the early twentieth century.
an-open-eyed-conspiracy-an-idyl-of-sarat:
William Dean Howells brings back his Basil March in this Saratoga idyl, printed in the author's edition at Edinburgh in 1898. On a hot day under the tall trees of Saratoga, March strolls to Congress Park after tea while Mrs. March stays fanning on the hotel verandah with the other ladies. In the park he falls in with a young pair.

The conspiracy of the title is an open-eyed one: March and others quietly help two young lovers whose families and circumstances stand in the way. Hotels, piazzas, and watering-place manners supply the comedy. Howells keeps the tale light and brief, a vacation piece from the dean of American letters, with his usual exact ear for American talk.
britannica-1911-alba-longa:
Alba Longa was an old city of Latium, set on the west edge of the Alban lake. It lay about 12 miles south-east of Rome. By the old tale, Ascanius set it up, and it was the oldest of all Latin cities. It was the mother of Rome, yet Rome, it is said, laid it waste under Tullus Hostilius. By that act Rome took the head place in the Latin league for itself.

Men who study old sites have set Alba Longa in more than one spot. Many place it between the Alban hill and the lake, at the house of Palazzolo. The article finds that spot unfit for an old city, and it does not match the words of Livy. Livy calls the city long, from its spread along a ridge.
britannica-1911-albenga:
Albenga, a town and bishop's see in Liguria, Italy, carries an old name: Album Ingaunum, chief town of the Ingauni. That tribe, one of the strongest in Liguria, held land as far as Genoa. The town stands on the north-west shore of the Gulf of Genoa, in Genoa province, and had 6,248 people in 1901.

Rome made it a municipium, and a carved record tells how Constantius rebuilt its walls, forum, and harbour in A.D. 354. East of town a Roman bridge still stands in good shape, near five hundred feet long with ten arches, on the old coast road. A tall pillar marker south of town may be a shrine rather than a tomb, since no door to a burial room shows. The town holds a fine Gothic cathedral of brick and an eight-sided baptistery with mosaic work on its vaults, dated to the eighth or ninth century.
britannica-1911-apollonius-of-perga:
Apollonius of Perga was a Greek geometer of the school of Alexandria. He was born about 262 B.C., some twenty-five years after Archimedes. He worked in the reigns of Ptolemy Euergetes and Ptolemy Philopator. His book on Conics won him the title of the Great Geometer, and his fame rests on that book. All his many other works have been lost, save one. We know them only by their titles and brief notes in later writers, above all Pappus.

The Conics was first written in eight books, then revised in a second edition. Books one and two were much changed at the call of Eudemus of Pergamum. The first three books went to Eudemus one by one, and the later books were given to King Attalus I after Eudemus died. Only four books live on in Greek, and three more in Arabic. The eighth book has never been found.
britannica-1911-azuaga:
Azuaga is a town of western Spain in the province of Badajoz, on the Belmez to Fuente del Arco railway, with 14,192 people in 1900. It serves as the central market for the livestock of broad upland pastures around it.

Two rivers water those pastures: the Matachel, a left-hand tributary of the Guadiana, and the Bembézar, a right-hand tributary of the Guadalquivir, so the town sits between two great river systems. Coarse woollen goods and pottery are made in Azuaga itself. Market, pasture, and small manufactures make up the whole of this short entry's account.
britannica-1911-beluga:
Beluga (Delphinapterus leucas), also called the white whale, is a member of the dolphin family known by its rounded head and even, light colour. It lives in Arctic seas and, in the west Atlantic, ranges as far south as the St Lawrence river, which it swims up for a good distance.

A beluga is almost pure white and grows to about twelve feet at most. Where other whales carry a back fin, it has only a low ridge along the back. Single animals have been taken on British coasts now and then. Some have also been kept alive for a time in tanks in America and in London, the entry notes.
britannica-1911-bucaramanga:
Bucaramanga, a city of Colombia and capital of the department of Santander, stands about 185 miles north-north-east of Bogotá on the Lebrija river, 3248 feet above sea level. Its population was estimated at 25,000 in 1902.

The 1911 Britannica entry sets the city in mountain country rich in gold, silver and iron mines, with fine coffee land in the valleys and on the lower slopes. It describes wide, straight streets, solid building, and many substantial public buildings. The whole article is brief, giving the city's position, height, setting and character rather than a history, and those are the facts it offers a reader.
britannica-1911-chattanooga:
Chattanooga is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a city in Tennessee, the county seat of Hamilton county. It stands on the Tennessee river near the Georgia boundary, about 150 miles south east of Nashville. Its population in the census of 1910 was 44,604. Many railways serve it, and steamboats work the river for eight months of the year. One of its lines, the old Memphis and Charleston, became famous in the Civil War.

The city occupies a striking site at a sharp bend of the river. Lookout Mountain rises to the south, its summit 2126 feet above the sea. Missionary Ridge rises to the east. Drives and electric lines reach both heights. The National Military Park on the Chickamauga battlefield covers 15 square miles. It was dedicated in 1895. In 1898 it served as a main mobilisation camp in the Spanish American War. Scenery and battlefield memory shape the entry's portrait of the city.
britannica-1911-conestoga:
The Conestoga were a tribe of North American Indians of Iroquoian stock. Their name is said to mean people of the immersed or forked poles. Their country lay in Pennsylvania and Maryland. It ran along the lower Susquehanna river and at the head of Chesapeake Bay. Men also knew them by the name Susquehannas.

In their strong days they could hold off the attacks of the Iroquois. That strength broke in 1675. The Iroquois then overwhelmed and scattered the tribe in full. Near a century of wandering followed that fall. The end came in the Indian wars of 1763. The tribe then suffered final extinction, in the entry's stark phrase. The hosted segment is brief and keeps to that arc. Power, defeat, wandering and end form its whole tale.
britannica-1911-coringa:
The 1911 Britannica article on Coringa describes a seaport of British India. It lies in the Godavari district of the Madras presidency. It stands on the estuary of a branch of the Godavari river. Its harbour is sheltered by Point Godavari. It once took vessels during the south-west monsoon. It was the most important harbour on that coast.

The account explains the port's decline. The harbour has silted up. It has lost its trade. Small coasting ships are still built and repaired nearby at Tallarevu. Two great storms struck the town. A flood in 1787 swept away most of it. A storm in 1832 wrecked it again. The Dutch settled there first. The English took the town in 1759.
britannica-1911-darbhanga:
Darbhanga is a town and district of British India in the Patna division of Bengal. The 1911 Britannica article gives the town a count of 66,244 in 1901. The town is a spread of villages grown up around the seat of its raja. That seat is a grand palace with gardens, a beast house, and a good library. A fine hospital, a market place, and a school serve the town.

The district runs from the Nepal frontier to the Ganges, on an area of 3,348 square miles. Its count in 1901 was 2,912,611 souls. The whole land is a flat plain of river silt. Rice is the staple crop, and the farmer leans most on the winter harvest. Ships of goods include indigo, linseed, saltpetre, and tobacco. Rail lines cross the district, some of them first laid as famine relief work in 1874.
britannica-1911-gonzaga:
Gonzaga names an Italian princely house, and the 1911 Britannica traces its rise at Mantua from the 13th century. The line took its name from the town where it likely began. In August 1328 Luigi the First drove out his brother-in-law Rinaldo Bonacolsi and became lord of Mantua. He held the post of captain general and then vicar general of the empire.

His son Guido seized Reggio from the Scaligeri in 1335 and held it till 1371. Later heads of the house mixed war with care for trade and town wealth. Giovan Francesco the Second won the title marquess of Mantua in 1432. Luigi the Third, called il Turco, was both a famed soldier and a patron of books and art. In 1530 Charles the Fifth raised the head of the house to duke of Mantua.
britannica-1911-latacunga:
Latacunga is a plateau town of Ecuador, capital of the province of Leon. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets it south of Quito at 9,141 feet. Two streams meet near it to form the Patate river. Its people were put at 12,000 in 1900, largely Indian. The old road and the railway between Guayaquil and Quito pass through it. Winds from snow clad heights make its air cold and harsh.

The town stands on bare, pumice strewn ground. Cotopaxi, a live volcano, looms only 25 miles away. Blasts from that peak have hurt the town more than once. Founded in 1534, it was wrecked by quakes four times between 1698 and 1798. Each time the town rose again on the same site. Ruins of an older native town nearby are said to date from the Incas.
britannica-1911-macugnaga: Macugnaga is the subject of a short village article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Macugnaga is a village in Piedmont in Italy, in the province of Novara. It lies west of a rail town that is itself south of Domodossola by rail. In 1901 its people numbered just under eight hundred. The village stands over four thousand feet above sea level. It lies northeast of the highest summit of Monte Rosa. Visitors frequent it as a summer resort.
britannica-1911-nanga: Nanga, the most primitive form of the ancient Egyptian harp, is the subject of a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its body was of wood, shaped like a boat or a vault. A sound bar ran down the back, with a round stick fixed on it for one end of the strings. The other end was tied to pegs in a curved neck. A nanga had only three or four strings, one note to each. Some can be seen at the British Museum.
britannica-1911-olga: Olga is the subject of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was the wife of Igor, prince of Kiev. After his death, from 945 she ruled as regent for her young son Sviatoslav. The entry records her baptism at Constantinople about 955 and her death about 969. It adds that she was later made a saint in the Russian church, her feast kept on the eleventh of July. A few lines fix the key facts of an early ruler of Kiev.
britannica-1911-onega:
Onega is the largest lake in Europe after Ladoga, with an area of 3,764 square miles, as this 1911 Britannica article describes it. It lies in the government of Olonets in European Russia, and sends its waters by the Svir into Lake Ladoga, so it belongs to the system of the Neva. Its basin runs north-west and south-east.

The lake's two parts differ sharply in form. The southern part has a fairly even outline and hardly any islands, while the northern part splits into many inlets and is crowded with islands and sunken rocks. That broken shore brings the coast line to 870 miles and makes sailing on the lake risky. The article goes on to the shores, the rocks found there, and the lake's depths, which reach past 400 feet in places.
britannica-1911-onondaga:
Onondaga is a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a tribe of North American Indians. The tribe was of Iroquoian stock and formed one of the Six Nations. Its home ground lay around the lake and creek of the same name in New York state.

The article says the tribe held a central place in the Iroquois league. The Onondaga kept the council fire for the league as a whole. Their land ran north to Lake Ontario and south to the Susquehanna river. The text traces a split in the 1700s, when part of the tribe backed the league and part moved to Canada. It closes with the groups left in Ontario and in New York.
britannica-1911-perino-del-vaga:
Perino del Vaga (1500–1547) was a painter of the Roman school, born near Florence in 1500. His true name was Perino Buonaccorsi. His father lost his wealth by gambling and became a soldier. His mother died when he was two months old, and his father's second wife then raised him. He was first placed with a druggist, then with a weak painter, Andrea da Ceri. At age eleven he passed to Ridolfo Ghirlandajo.

Perino soon passed his fellow pupils, and he studied Michelangelo's great cartoon with care. A painter named Vaga then took charge of the boy and set him to work at Toscanella. When Perino at last reached Rome, he was poor, with no clear hope but work for trade decorators. Still, he studied Michelangelo and the antique with zeal. In time he was trusted with part of the work of greater men.
britannica-1911-saiga: Saiga is a desert antelope, described in a brief nature entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is known by its swollen, puffy nose, with nostril holes that point down. Male horns are ringed and amber in colour. The coat is white in winter and sandy in summer. Its home ground was the Kirghiz Steppes, though its range once reached west to Poland. Fossils show it once ranged across western Europe.
britannica-1911-talladega:
Talladega is a city in Alabama and the seat of Talladega county, east of Birmingham. It stands in the foothills of the Blue Ridge, about five hundred sixty feet above sea level. Its people numbered five thousand eight hundred fifty four in nineteen ten. Three rail lines serve the city. Limestone and coal are found in the country near it, and mineral springs lie close by.

The city holds a college for women and Talladega College, opened in eighteen sixty seven. That college was the first in the state for the higher schooling of Black students. Schools for deaf, blind, and mute pupils also stand there. Its works make cotton goods, cotton seed oil, iron, and hosiery. Talladega was first an Indian village, and a famed battle was fought there in eighteen thirteen.
britannica-1911-tanga:
Tanga, whose name means the sail, is a seaport of German East Africa. It lies across from the island of Pemba, on the south shore of Tanga Bay. The town is laid out in a regular plan on high ground and holds about 6,000 people. Its public buildings include the chief officer's house, a hospital, and a barracks. There are Protestant and Catholic churches, plus state and mission schools.

Tanga serves as the port of the Usambara district, where many farms thrive. Ships enter the harbour by a broad channel five to eight fathoms deep. German mail steamers call at the port. A railway also starts at Tanga and runs to the Usambara highlands. The article thus shows a small port town with a clear role as a trade and rail head for its district.
britannica-1911-tonga:
Tonga, also called the Friendly Islands from a name given by Captain Cook, is a chain of islands in the South Pacific, and this 1911 Britannica entry maps it in detail. The chain lies south-west of Samoa and east of Fiji and holds about 150 islands, though their land adds up to only 385 square miles. They fall into three groups: Tonga in the south, Hapai in the middle, and Vavau in the north. The biggest island is Tongatabu, which holds the capital, Nukualofa.

Most of the islands are low coral land, seldom rising far above the sea, with rich soil and lush plant growth. Some in the west are volcanic and much higher, and a few are still active. East of the whole chain runs a deep trough in the ocean floor that stretches toward New Zealand.
britannica-1911-velez-malaga:
Vélez-Málaga, a town of south Spain, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in the province of Malaga, in a rich valley at the foot of a high sierra. The small river Vélez runs by it, a mile from the sea. In 1900 it held a little over twenty-three thousand people.

The town was once a place of great trade, but its wealth has much declined. No rail line reaches it, and quakes in 1884 and floods in 1907 hit it hard. The growth round it is thick and lush, from aloes and palms to cane, vine, and olive. The Moors held the town from 711 to 1487, when Ferdinand of Castile took it. Their citadel made it a fort and a post of trade. Its river mouth gives good anchorage for ships.
britannica-1911-wagga-wagga:
Wagga-Wagga is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Wagga-Wagga is a town in New South Wales, Australia. It stands on the left bank of the River Murrumbidgee. Rail lines place it west of Sydney and north-east of Melbourne.

A steel viaduct carries the crossing over the river at the town. Its approaches are formed by heavy embankments. The entry lists a school of art with a library and a fine convent on Mount Erin. A good racecourse and show grounds are also named. Some gold mining went on in the district, but the land was chiefly pastoral. Cereals, tobacco, and wine were also produced in fair amounts. The article is a brief sketch of a river town serving a farming and grazing country.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albenga:
The Diocese of Albenga in Italy takes in seventy-nine towns in the province of Porto Maurizio and forty-five more in the province of Genoa, under the Archdiocese of Genoa. Legend places the martyrdom of St. Calocero of Brescia at Albenga between 121 and 125. The entry warns that the accounts of his death are not historically verified. The first bishop known with certainty is Quintius, who signed a synodal letter in 451 backing the condemnation of Nestorius and Eutyches.

Albenga's scale in the entry's day was large: 170 parishes, 485 secular priests, 86 regulars, meaning priests in religious orders, and 354 churches and chapels serving about 119,280 people. The entry closes by listing its sources, from Ughelli's Italia sacra of 1722 to nineteenth-century local histories of the city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-albrec: Albert, Bishop of Riga and Apostle of Livonia, died in January 1229. When the people of Livonia twice fell away from Christianity, he organized a crusade and sailed up the Duna in April 1200 with twenty-three ships. He founded Riga in 1201 and became its bishop. He set up the Order of the Knights of the Sword in 1202 as a standing army. He finished converting the country before 1206 and raised the bishoprics of Semgall-Kurland, Dorpat, and Oesel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alonso-de-erc:
Alonso de Ercilla y Zúñiga was a Spanish soldier and poet, born at Madrid in 1533 and dead there in 1594. His mother, lady-in-waiting to the Infanta María, made the fatherless Alonso a page to Prince Philip. Learned teachers, extensive travel, and court life educated him. At fifteen he toured Italy and Germany with Philip for three years.

Ercilla sailed for America with Alderete in October 1555, with Philip's leave. Alderete died near Panamá in April 1556, but Ercilla reached Peru. In 1557 he joined Chile's new Governor, García Hurtado de Mendoza. For two or three years he fought the Arauco insurrection brilliantly, distinguishing himself in battle. After illness he returned to Spain in 1562 and married in 1570. La Araucana, his great work, is an epic of thirty-seven cantos on Spanish difficulties in Arauco. It tells heroic deeds of natives and companions. He died at Madrid neglected and poor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alpha-and-ome:
Alpha and Omega, in Jewish theology, express God's eternity through the first and last letters of the alphabet. When God passed before Moses on Sinai, the Law-giver called out: Jehovah, Jehovah, merciful God, slow to anger, and abounding in goodness and truth. Goodness and truth fill God's being, foremost among his moral attributes.

In Christian usage, expressing God's eternity by the first and last letters seems to have passed from the synagogue into the Church. Hebrew Aleph and Thaw gave way to Alpha and Omega, but the substitution inevitably lost some meaning and beauty. The Greek letters bear no relation to the Hebrew word for Truth, which Aleph and Thaw begin and end.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andreas-de-ve:
Andreas de Vega, theologian and Franciscan Observantine, was born at Segovia in Spain, at an unknown date, and died at Salamanca probably in 1560. He studied and taught at the University of Salamanca before becoming an Observantine Franciscan. He kept teaching in the Observantine monastery, where Alphonso de Castro also taught. Both won distinction in speculative theology. Vega was a moderate Scotist holding to Saint Bonaventure.

Emperor Charles V sent Vega as a theologian to the Council of Trent. There he worked with Cardinal Petrus Pacheco, Bishop of Jaen, patron of the Franciscan order. Vega stood out in debates on the canon of Scripture and the Vulgate, settled in the fourth session's decree on 8 April 1546. In debates on justification he argued against Dominicus de Soto, defender of rigid Thomism. The justification decree followed in the sixth session on 13 January 1547. Before the council he had defended Catholic justification against the Protestants.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-astorga:
Astorga, in Latin Asturica Augusta, suffragan of Valladolid in Spain, is said to date from the third century. It was the chief church of the Asturias in 344, following a long eclipse became an episcopal see again in 747, and shows a regular succession of bishops since 841. At different times it answered to Braga and to Santiago.

It covers the entire province of Leon and numbers 300,115 Catholics, 990 parishes, each with its own church, 431 chapels, and 1,183 priests. The entry is a diocesan record: a Roman town's church, eclipsed and restored, holding a regular bishops' list for over a thousand years and a vast parish network across Leon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-braga:
Braga, in Portugal's Minho province between the Este and Cavado rivers, takes its name from the knee-length bragas worn by its ancient people. Romans called such dress barbarous, and the city, Bracara Augusta, grew into Galicia's metropolis and a chief city of Lusitania. Augustus joined it to Hispania Tarraconensis and made it a judicial center.

Tradition says Peter de Rates, disciple of James, preached there, though the Bollandists call it pure tradition. Paternus certainly held the see about 390. After Astorga's fall in 433, Braga rose to metropolitan rank under Leo I, kept supremacy until the Muslim invasion of 711, and regained it from Paschal II in 1110. It later contested Toledo for Spain's primacy and lost.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caughnawaga:
Caughnawaga, or Sault St. Louis, was an Iroquois reservation just above Montreal, on the St. Lawrence's south bank, covering 12,327 acres. In 1905 it counted 2,100 people, all Catholics except five or six families, speaking the Mohawk dialect. The Sault had been granted to the Jesuits as a seigniory in 1680.

The settlement began when P. Raffeix gathered Christian Iroquois converts on the St. Lawrence to shield them from persecution and temptation in their home villages. Seven communities settled at Laprairie in 1667, the mission moved upriver in 1676, and that second site saw Catherine Tegakwitha's holy life and death in 1680. A granite monument was raised there in 1890.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-councils-of-b:
A substantial reference entry recounts the many councils held at Braga in Portugal, several of which shaped worship and discipline across the early medieval Church in Iberia. It weighs the doubtful council of 411, probably invented, against well-attested meetings whose decrees survive in detail.

The council of 563 ordered one common rite, uniform lessons at vigils and solemn Mass, and rules on baptism, ordination, singing, and burial, while guarding against Priscillianist error. The second council of 572 increased the number of bishops in Galicia, and later meetings down to the sixteenth century handled clergy discipline and church property. Readers gain a clear sense of how Braga's bishops governed a growing Christian region.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ercole-gonzag:
Ercole Gonzaga, a cardinal, was born at Mantua on 23 November 1505 and died on 2 March 1563. Bologna gave him his philosophy studies under Pomponazzi, and theology came later. His uncle Sigismondo gave up the See of Mantua in his favour in 1520, or as some say 1525. The insignia of the cardinalate reached him in 1527, brought back from Rome by his mother Isabella.

Young as he was, church reform drew his zeal, above all in his own diocese, with help from his friend Cardinal Giberti of Verona. His life was stainless, and his manuscript Vitae Christianae institutio witnesses to his piety. A Latin catechism for his diocese's priests came from his press, and he built the diocesan seminary, carrying out reforms urged by the Council of Trent. His charity knew no bounds, and many talented young men had their university expenses paid by him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fray-tomas-de:
Tomás de Berlanga, a Dominican bishop of Panama, was drawn into the quarrel between Pizarro and Almagro over Peru. At Rome in 1528 he won a separate Dominican province of Santa Cruz. He became its provincial in 1530 and clashed with Domingo Betanzos over the new Mexican province. Soon after, he took up the vast Panama see, which covered the whole west coast of South America.

The crown sent Berlanga to settle the dispute between the two conquerors and to report on Peru. He found his task already undone, since Pizarro had sent Almagro off to Chile, so no hearing could take place. He refused Pizarro's overtures and sent home a blunt report of what he had seen. He kept only a dozen silver spoons for himself and gave the rest of his gifts to hospitals in Panama and Nicaragua.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frederic-bara:
Frederic Baraga, the first bishop of Marquette, Michigan, left Austria in 1830 to spend the rest of his life among the native peoples of the upper Great Lakes. Born in Carniola in 1797, he studied law at Vienna. He then turned to the priesthood and was ordained in 1823. After two months at sea he landed in New York on the last day of 1830 and made his way to Cincinnati.

His first mission, at Arbre Croche, brought more than five hundred baptisms in under three years. Later posts at Grand River, La Pointe, and L'Anse added hundreds more among the Ottawa and Chippewa. The entry follows a tireless traveler who built plain churches and schools with scant funds. In 1853 he became bishop of a new diocese that matched the field he had already worked.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-girolamo-geng:
Girolamo Genga was a painter born at Urbino in 1476, who died there in 1551. Apprenticed at fifteen to Luca Signorelli, whom he assisted at Orvieto, he then spent three years in Perugino's school and became the intimate friend of Raphael. A Catholic Encyclopedia article presents a talented craftsman of many gifts.

After time in Florence and Siena he returned to Urbino for Duke Guidobaldo II. He then worked at Rome, painting an altar-piece for Saint Catherine of Siena. He later returned to Urbino at Duke Francesco Maria's request, followed him into banishment at Cesena, and painted his chief altar-piece, now in the Brera at Milan. Beyond painting and sculpture he modeled in wax, clay, and terra-cotta, designed vestments and musical instruments, and played music admirably.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jorgen-zoega:
Jorgen Zoega was a Danish archaeologist and numismatist ranked with Winckelmann and Visconti as a founder of scientific archaeology. Born near Tonder in northern Schleswig in 1755 to a Protestant pastor of Italian descent, he studied philosophy and classics at Gottingen and Leipzig. Repeated journeys to Italy awakened his archaeological passion.

A Danish pension brought him to Vienna, where he studied under the numismatist Eckhel, and to Rome in 1783, where Cardinal Borgia welcomed him. Cataloguing Borgia's fine coin collection, he won a papal pension and Danish support. He became Danish consul at Rome in 1798, and turned from coins to Egyptian and Coptic studies. By penetration and sound judgment he pointed later scholars toward the interpretation of hieroglyphics, and Berlin and Vienna elected him to their academies in 1806.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-anton-:
Joseph Anton Sambuga was a German priest and theologian who taught Bavaria's royal children. Born at Walldorf near Heidelberg in 1752 to Italian parents, he studied at Mannheim, Wiesloch, and Heidelberg, then finished theology in Italy and was ordained at Como in 1774. He served as chaplain and court preacher at Mannheim.

In 1797 he became religion teacher to Prince Louis, the future King Louis I of Bavaria, and followed the court to Munich. A friend of the theologian Sailer, he wrote on celibacy, on the dangers of shallow philosophy, and on the nature of the Church. Posthumous volumes gathered his sermons, letters, and reflections.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-de-zumar:
Juan de Zumárraga was the first Bishop of Mexico and Protector of the Indians. Born at Durango in 1468, he joined the Franciscans and was chosen bishop-elect in 1527. He reached Mexico in December 1528 to find the colony's auditors taxing, enslaving, and branding Indians, and he fought them with only spiritual weapons.

Zumárraga placed the city under interdict in 1530 after the auditors seized a priest from a church. Consecrated at Valladolid in 1533, he returned to a more peaceful colony, where tradition dates the apparition of Our Lady of Guadalupe to December 1531. He died in Mexico in 1548, having built the new Church amid turmoil.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-malaga:
Malaga was a diocese in Spain, made a suffragan of Granada by the Concordat of 1851. Before that it had depended on Seville. The city itself was ancient Malaka, known to Strabo and Ptolemy. It mattered under Carthage, then as a Roman municipium, and under the Visigoths it became a bishop's see.

Its earliest known bishop was Patricius, consecrated about 290. Arabs took the city after Guadalete, and the bishopric lapsed. Ferdinand and Isabella retook it in 1487 after hard resistance, and restored the see. Its cathedral, begun in 1528 on a former mosque site, was finished in 1719. By 1910 the diocese counted 520,000 Catholics, 123 parishes, 481 priests, and 200 churches and chapels, with colleges, schools, and convents across its towns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pablo-jose-ar:
Pablo Jose Arriaga was a Jesuit missionary in Peru, born at Vergara in Biscay in 1564. He joined the Society of Jesus in 1579 and reached Peru in 1585, where he was ordained. In 1588 he became rector of the College of San Martin at Lima, a post he held three times across twenty-four years. In 1601 his superiors sent him to Rome, his first European trip.

From 1604 to 1622 Arriaga led the drive to root out surviving native idolatry in Peru, travelling with early official visitor Fernando de Avendano. He built a college for sons of Indian chiefs and a house of correction for native shamans. In 1620 he finished his Extirpation of Idolatry in Peru, printed at Lima in 1621. Sent to Europe again in 1621, he died at a ship's helm in a storm off Porto Bello, holding a crucifix before his fellow passengers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pedro-d-alva-:
Pedro d'Alva y Astorga was a Friar Minor of the Strict Observance and a voluminous theological writer. He generally defended the Immaculate Conception. Born at Carbajales in Spain toward the sixteenth century's end, he died in Belgium in 1667. He joined the Franciscans in Peru. He lectured on theology, served as the Franciscans' procurator-general at Rome, and as qualificator of the Holy Office. He travelled tirelessly.

His chief opponents were the Dominicans. His polemic ran so personal and violent that he was banished to the Low Countries. Two editions of his Nodus indissolubilis on the concept of mind and concept of womb, Madrid 1661 and 1663, stand on the Index of prohibited books. His writings run to forty folio volumes. Most important is his Seraphic Arsenal for defending the Immaculate Conception's title, Madrid 1648, written with the Friars Minor's best theologians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-skarga:
Peter Skarga was a Polish Jesuit theologian, missionary, and court preacher, born at Grójec in 1536. Schooled at home, Cracow, and Warsaw, he tutored at Vienna, took orders in 1564, and preached his famous sermons as canon of Lwów, converting Protestants. Entering the Society in 1568, he served as Polish penitentiary at St. Peter's in Rome, then worked the colleges of Pułtusk and Wilno.

His 1576 treatise On the Unity of the Church of God pressed schismatics toward union and still stands in high esteem. Stephen Báthori prized him, made him rector of the Wilno academy founded in 1578, and took him on campaign. At Cracow from 1584 he founded the Brotherhood of Mercy and a pawnshop for the poor. Court preacher to Sigismund III for twenty-four years from 1588, he helped unite the Ruthenian Church with Rome in 1596. He died at Cracow in 1612.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-phasga:
Phasga, called Pisgah in the Authorized Version, was a mountain of the Abarim range east of the Jordan, in Moab, facing Jericho. Whether the Hebrew word is a proper name or a common noun remains unclear. The biblical markers agree: it stands above the desert's edge, east of the Dead Sea's northern end, beside Mount Nebo. It guards the south-east border of the Holy Land and commands a wide view.

Three scenes fix it in Israel's story. On its slopes the people camped, in its field of Sophim Balaam spoke his second oracle over Israel, and from its summit Moses surveyed the Promised Land he would not enter. The entry concludes that Phasga is Mount Nebo itself, or better its western peak, Ras Siâghâ, south-west of Hesban.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pietro-maria-:
Pietro Maria Gazzaniga was an Italian Dominican theologian who defended the teaching of Saint Thomas Aquinas in eighteenth-century Austria. He was born at Bergamo in 1722 and entered the Dominicans young. He taught philosophy and church history in his order's houses, and then at the University of Bologna.

Called to Vienna in 1760 to fill the Dominican chair of dogmatic theology, he drew students from all quarters, including the Empress Maria Theresa and the future Pius VI. He spent twenty years there. By steady loyalty to Thomas he won over allies and restored Thomism in the Austrian schools against reformers who wanted them freer of church control. He died at Vicenza in 1799.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scipione-gonz:
Scipione Gonzaga, cardinal, was born at Mantua on 11 November 1542 and died at San Martino on 11 January 1593. From the dukes of Sabbioneta's family, he grew up under Cardinal Ercole Gonzaga and advanced fast in Greek and Latin. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a patron of letters through courts and lawsuits.

At Bologna and later Padua he studied mathematics and philosophy, founding at Padua the Academy of the Ethereals. All his life he backed writers, among them Tasso, who sought his counsel on Jerusalem Delivered, and Guarino, who dedicated Pastor Fido to him. After theology he went to Rome, became secret chamberlain to Pius IV, and took priestly orders. A lawsuit with Mantua's duke under Gregory XIII ended in reconciliation, and Guise backing made him bishop of Mende in France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-aloysius-g:
St. Aloysius Gonzaga was born in the castle of Castiglione on 9 March 1568 and died on 21 June 1591, a young nobleman who gave up an inheritance for the Jesuits. This entry follows a boy placed at eight in the court of Francesco de' Medici at Florence, then at Mantua, who at twelve came under St. Charles Borromeo at Brescia and received First Communion from him.

In 1581 he went with his father to Spain, where he and his brother became pages to James, son of Philip II. There he resolved to become a Jesuit, though he first considered the Discalced Carmelites. Returning to Italy in 1584, he won his father's hard consent. He renounced his heritage for his brother in 1585, with the emperor's approval, before presenting himself to the Jesuit general.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-amalberga:
St. Amalberga, otherwise Amelia, was a saint whose records are, this entry warns, in very great confusion, and sorting her out is half the point. Related somehow to Pepin of Landen, sister or niece the Bollandists cannot say, she married Witger and became mother of three saints, Gudila, Reinelda, and Emembertus. Norman chroniclers' claim of a second marriage seems erroneous.

Pharailda and Ermelende, the entry adds, are not admitted as her children by the Bollandists. Husband and wife at last withdrew from the world, he to become a monk and she a nun. Two further Amalbergas, a virgin a century later and another in the twelfth, deepen the tangle, and the first two are celebrated together on 10 July.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-fructuosus:
Fructuosus of Braga, greatest of Spain's monastic bishops, planted ten monasteries and a house for eighty virgins. Son of a Gothic general, he studied at Palencia, then withdrew as a hermit to a Galician desert after his parents' death. Pupils gathered until the monastery of Complutum rose, which he first ruled himself, then handed to an abbot before returning to the desert. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 16 April, about 665.

Called to Dumium in 654 and to Braga's archbishopric on 1 December 656, he governed from a monk's experience. Abbot Valerius wrote his life from his pupils' accounts. In 1102 his relics moved to Compostela. He is pictured with a stag he saved from hunters, and two monastic rules survive from his hand. The entry joins hermit, founder, and archbishop in one career.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-martin-of-:
Martin of Braga, a sixth-century bishop and ecclesiastical writer, leads this Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in Pannonia around 520, he went on pilgrimage to the Holy Land. There he took up monastic life. Spanish pilgrims then drew him to Galicia in north-west Spain. He arrived in 550, hoping to win over the Suevi, who mixed lingering pagan customs with Arian belief.

From abbot of Dumio he rose to bishop, then to archbishop of Braga. He chaired the second Council of Braga in 572. His writings run chiefly to short works on conduct, worship, and the disciplined life. They include a guide to honest living built on the four cardinal virtues. They also include a collection of eighty-four canons that later counted for medieval church law. Gregory of Tours praised his learning, and his feast falls on 20 March.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-notburga:
Notburga, patroness of servants and peasants, worked as a cook in Tyrol and gave her own food to the poor. Born about 1265 at Rattenberg on the Inn, she served Count Henry of Rothenburg. Her mistress Ottilia ordered leftovers fed to swine, so Notburga saved portions of her own meals, especially on Fridays, and carried them to hungry neighbours.

Legend tells how food in her bundle turned to shavings and wine to vinegar when her master challenged her. It also tells how her sickle hung in the air when a peasant master kept her from church. Dismissed and rehired, she died about 16 September 1313, asking burial wherever oxen drawing her corpse should halt. The entry blends household charity with the folklore of a servant saint.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-sexburga:
Sexburga, queen of Kent turned abbess, founded Minster in Sheppey and later ruled Ely. Daughter of Anna, king of the East Angles, she married Earconbert of Kent about 640 and lived with him twenty-four years. Her sons Egbert and Lothar both became kings of Kent, and her daughters Earcongota and Ermenhild both became nuns and saints.

Widowed in 664, she founded the abbey of Minster in Sheppey. After a few years she moved to Ely and placed herself under her sister Etheldreda, then abbess. When Etheldreda died, probably in 679, Sexburga was elected in her place. In 695 she presided over moving Etheldreda's relics to a new shrine with a white marble sarcophagus. She died about 699.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-walburga:
Walburga, an English abbess in Germany, carried Wimborne learning to Franconia beside her brothers. Born in Devonshire about 710, daughter of Richard, an under-king of the West Saxons, and Winna, sister of Boniface, she had brothers Willibald and Winibald. When Richard left with his sons on pilgrimage to the Holy Land, eleven-year-old Walburga was entrusted to Wimborne's abbess.

Twenty-six years in Wimborne's school and community, famed for holiness and stern discipline, trained her in solid learning. Later she wrote Winibald's Life and a Latin account of Willibald's travels in Palestine, counting among the first English women writers. Called to Germany, she ruled Heidenheim's double monastery. She died there on 25 February 777, patroness of Eichstätt and protector against hydrophobia and storms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thugga:
Thugga, a titular see of Numidia, is now Dougga, a village in Tunisia famous for its ruins. It may be the Numidian fortress Tocai named by Diodorus about 305 BC. King Masinissa probably took it from Carthage in the second century BC. Under Rome it grew from a pagus dependent on Carthage to a municipium under Septimius Severus and a colony in 261.

Justinian's fortress there still partly stands. Because Thugga held both a pagus and a civitas, it had two bishops at once. Saturninus and Honoratus attended the Council of Carthage in 256, and a Donatist bishop, Paschasius, attended Carthage in 411. Its ruins include a Capitol temple built under Marcus Aurelius, a theatre, three triumphal arches, Roman tombs and a Punic mausoleum.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vaga:
Vaga was a titular see of Numidia, often named by historians and ancient geographers. Before Rome's conquest it ranked as an important trading centre. Handed to the Carthaginians by Massinissa, it joined the Numidian kingdom and later Numidia Proconsularis. Metellus destroyed it, but it soon rose from ruin, and under Septimius Severus it was called Colonia Septimia Vaga.

Justinian fortified it and renamed it Theodorias in honour of his wife Theodora. Today it is the small city of Beja, centre of a civil district of about 100,000 people in Tunisia, and a railway station in a rich farming region. Justinian's halls still stand, much altered, and the great tower of the kasba was the old citadel's keep. The entry sketches a town that outlived empires.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-bartholom:
Bartholomew of Braga, born Bartholomew Fernandez at Verdela near Lisbon in May 1514, died at Viana on 16 July 1590. Later called a Martyribus for the church of his baptism, he came of humble parents. He joined the Dominicans on 11 November 1527 and was professed on 20 November 1529. After his studies he taught philosophy at Lisbon, then theology for about twenty years in various houses of his order.

In 1551 he took his master's degree at Salamanca's provincial chapter. While teaching at Batalha he was called to Évora by the Infante Dom Luis to guide the religious schooling of his son Dom Antonio, a task that took two years. In 1558, against his own wish and purely from obedience, he was named Archbishop of Braga. The entry follows his reforming episcopate and his retirement to Viana.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zamboanga:
Zamboanga is the Philippine diocese covering Basilan, Camiguin, Dinagat, Mindanao, Siargao, and the Sulu Archipelago across 39,000 square miles for about 670,000 people. Its Catholics number 290,000 beside 300,000 Moro Muslim Malays and 80,000 pagans of varied tribes. Jesuits and Recollects evangelized Mindanao from the late sixteenth century, and members of both orders died at fanatical Moro hands.

When Jesuits returned, their Mindanao labours among wild tribes and even Moros won success, and their Tamontaca home for abandoned Moro children echoed Paraguay's Reductions. Spain funded priests and missions, so American cession in 1898 struck evangelization hard: many Jesuits were recalled and posts abandoned. Today sixty mission parishes and forty-five priests, mostly Jesuits, serve the diocese, with Sacred Heart missionaries in Surigao province and native Mary sisters teaching in larger towns. Pius X erected the see by Bull of 10 April 1910, with Michael O'Doherty, rector of Salamanca's Irish College, as first bishop.
doe-osti-2574314-non-catalytic-pyrolysis:
Pre-FEED study DE-FE0032234, from the University of North Dakota under Junior Nasah with H Quest Vanguard, covers May 2023 to April 2025. At a working Bakken oil pad, about 54,000 standard cubic feet of associated gas is flared each day. The study designs a plant to convert that gas into hydrogen and high-value carbon black by microwave plasma pyrolysis, with no carbon dioxide produced.

Three units make up the design. A microwave pyrolysis unit uses H Quest's proprietary process to crack the gas. A patent-pending gas conditioning unit, designed by the university, smooths the pad's intermittent, variable flow first. An auxiliary unit burns some gas to power the other two in island mode, off the grid. Lab tests with simulated Bakken gas set the energy needs and conversion rates. A techno-economic assessment then prices the whole package for that host site.
doe-osti-2998008-assessing-edge-localize:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory final report ORNL/TM-2025/4252 closes cooperative project NFE-22-09320 for Commonwealth Fusion Systems' SPARC tokamak. Authors Andreas Wingen, Andreas Kleiner, Tom Looby, and co-authors, dated September 2025, study a plasma edge problem. Edge localized modes, or ELMs, are bursts that dump heat onto the vessel wall. In SPARC's low-collisionality high-performance shots they could damage the machine.

One fix is to fire frozen pellets that trigger small ELMs early and often, draining energy in sips instead of gulps. Injection paths from the high-field side and the low-field side are both drawn into the design. Linear stability runs with the M3D-C1 code, built on a chosen equilibrium, test whether pellet pacing can hold the edge stable. The report gives SPARC's team a modeled basis for the pellet system's settings.
doe-osti-3002040-assessing-edge-localize: ELM mitigation got pellet-triggered, and this DOE report tests the affordable compact approach. The pages detail the findings. The fusion folks get their data. The modes were edge localized. The triggering was pellet. The folks were fusion. The data were fusion.
doe-osti-3018026-dual-loop-solvent-based:
Xin Gao, Jinwen Wang, and Kunlei Liu of the University of Kentucky wrote this final technical report for award DE-FE0032134, issued February 2026. The reporting period ran from March 2022 to November 2025. Partners included PPL Corporation, the Electric Power Research Institute, and ALL4. The project developed a dual-loop, solvent-based carbon capture system aiming at net negative emissions at lower cost.

Two loops give the design its options: the primary loop uses a water-lean solvent, and the pair can be tuned for capture duty and cost. Bench trials characterized what the solvent becomes as it ages. The report tabulates degradation products for the primary loop solvent, and sizes their load in wastewater. The design basis assumes 353 gallons per minute of wastewater discharge. Permitting analysis runs throughout, including what regulators would need for ammonia, metals, and toxicity. Capture developers get the chemistry and the paperwork reality in one volume.
doe-osti-3377784-high-efficacy-validatio:
High Efficacy Validation of Hydride MEGA Tanks at the ARIES Lab is the final report for cooperative research agreement CRD-21-18281, issued as NLR/TP-5700-99328 in June 2026. Katherine Hurst is the National Laboratory of the Rockies technical contact, with Michael Cox and Joe Leiva named in the evidence record. The project validated a GKN metal hydride hydrogen storage system, described as a first-of-its-kind capability.

The report concentrates on getting the system installed and approved safely. Because the fire code was not straightforward for this technology, the team worked with environment, health, and safety staff and the NFPA 2 hydrogen code committee. A setback of 45 feet from the hazardous zone was recalculated down to 15 feet, reflecting the system's lower storage pressure, and piping diagrams were drawn to match.
doe-osti-3683858-rational-development-of:
Final report for award DE-FE0031736, submitted September 5, 2026, covers membranes for capturing carbon dioxide. Haiqing Lin of the State University of New York at Buffalo was principal investigator. The project period ran from July 2019 to December 2023. The goal was a membrane that lets carbon dioxide through fast while holding back nitrogen and oxygen. 

Mixed matrix films paired rubbery, polar polymers with soluble metal-organic cage fillers. Early films passed the carbon dioxide marks for flow and for both selectivity pairs at room heat. Thin-film composite versions then reached the full permeance and nitrogen selectivity targets. The report is candid that repeat runs still vary too much. Polymer and cage making was scaled up to batches of ten to twenty grams. Roll-to-roll film making was not fully tuned in the time left. Models for gas uptake in the polymers were also built.
eirik-the-red-s-saga:
The Reverend J. Sephton read his translation of Eirik the Red's Saga before the Literary and Philosophical Society of Liverpool on January 12, 1880, and D. Marples and Company printed it that year. Fifteen short chapters carry the Norse story from Olaf the White, king in Dublin, to the settlers of Iceland and Greenland.

The saga follows Eirik's discovery of Greenland, his son Leif's finding of Vinland, and the widow Gudrid's two marriages. Karlsefni's party winters at Straumsfjordr and at Hop, trades and fights with the Skroelingar, and loses Thorvald to a one-footed archer. One scene describes the natives' hooded garment, open at the sides and fastened between the legs. Bjarni's heroic fate closes the tale, and Gudrid's descendants end it. Sephton's plain rendering put the Vinland voyages before English readers in a cheap, readable form.
fritiofs-saga:
Tegner wrote Sweden's great national epic poem, Fritiofs Saga. Its hero is Fritiof, a bold sea rover of the old North. The poem follows his love, his exile, and his voyages. Norse gods and old temples frame the action. Balder's temple holds a key place in the story.

This volume is a school edition of the Swedish text. Andrew Stomberg edited it for American students. His introduction places the poem in Swedish literature. A bibliography, notes, and a full vocabulary support the reading. The notes explain the many mythic names in the verse. Students get the poem itself plus the tools to read it in Swedish. The edition served colleges and high schools alike.
nasa-tm-19660023431-a-theoretical-and-ex:
James R Sterrett and John B Barber at Langley joined theory with experiment on jets that blow sideways into a Mach 6 stream, in a paper given in Brussels in May 1966. A secondary jet can steer a vehicle or protect a surface. Where it enters, the main stream separates ahead of the jet and forms a complex pattern. The structure of that jet and its upstream separation are their stated focus.

At six times the speed of sound, the flow is firmly hypersonic. Small jets then have outsized effects on heating and pressure. Experiments anchor the theory in measured flow patterns. Control jets were a live option for missiles and entry vehicles, which made the pair's careful account valuable to designers.
nasa-tm-19670014147-on-the-calculation-o:
N. Ya. Vovchenko wrote this paper in Moscow, where it appeared in 1965 in a Russian engineering volume from a Moscow publishing house. The English version was issued at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, in December 1966. Its subject is the calculation of an inertial navigation system, which guides a vehicle near Earth by sensing its own motion.

Vovchenko treats a geometrical system with two platforms. One gyrostabilized platform holds its orientation against inertial space using three integrating float gyroscopes. A second platform carries accelerometers, imitates the geographical coordinate frame, and is driven to the local vertical like a Schuler pendulum. The paper sharpens the dynamics equations given in earlier work. It also evaluates the systematic errors caused by translational and Coriolis accelerations, and follows the system as the vehicle moves along a great circle.
nasa-tm-19680016459-effects-of-salts-on-:
Mary K. Johnson, Robert D. McElroy, and Emmett J. Johnson of Ames Research Center study a salt-loving alga in this paper, the second in a series. The green alga Dunaliella viridis thrives where salt levels would kill most plants. The authors test how salts affect its growth.

Parts of the work were presented at microbiology meetings in Moscow in 1966 and New York in 1967. The team found the range of salt concentrations allowing growth was very broad. The cells' previous history shifted that range slightly, but in a significant way. Findings like these help explain how life persists in briny waters. They also inform NASA studies of life in extreme environments.
nasa-tm-19680018163-the-role-of-radiatio:
Cyril Ponnamperuma of the Ames Research Center looks at what radiation did in the first making of organic compounds on Earth. Many ideas link the start of life to a long span of slow chemical change first. Simple organic matter grew more complex over time, gaining new traits as its atoms took new forms.

Ponnamperuma draws on the early work of Oparin on that slow process. He asks how much of life's raw stock radiation could have made on the young Earth. Sunlight, heat, and electric sparks were rival energy sources at the time. The paper weighs radiation's share among them. It also frames tests that check each source on gas mixes like those of the early Earth.
podcast-dannyjones-sJ46Vz7SVgA:
Philosopher Jason Jorjani returns to Danny Jones for a talk that links Epstein, Atlantis, and what may hide under Antarctica. Jorjani is known for grand theories that tie myth to power. Jones gives him a wide field here.

Jorjani lays out how he thinks the Epstein case, the lost city tale, and the sealed ice of the far south fit one frame. He names the bases, the trips, and the old Nazi lore he draws on. Jones asks what holds the frame off the ground. Listeners get a dense weave of three dark tales. The library files the talk as an archive record.
samantha-at-saratoga: Marietta Holley wrote Samantha at Saratoga, given by the author, as comrade and fellow wanderer, to the great army of summer tramps. A note at the head gives Holley's life dates as 1836 to 1926. It calls her America's first female humorist, a popular author and a well-known suffragette. She first issued books as Josiah Allen's Wife. The contents list a preface and sixteen chapters, opening with Samantha at Saratoga, Ardelia Tutt and Her Mother, and The Charity of the Jonesvillians.
the-healthy-life-vol-v-nos-24-28-the-ind: The Healthy Life, described as the independent health magazine, is shown here in Volume V, covering July to December 1913 and published in London at Graham House, Tudor Street. An index for the volume lists pieces such as A Ballade of Skyfaring by S. Gertrude Ford, On Learning to Breathe by Dr J. Stenson Hooker, Camping Out by C. R. Freeman, and Care of Cupboards by Florence Daniel. Only the title page and the start of the index are present here, so the magazine articles themselves do not appear.
the-saga-of-grettir-the-strong-grettir-s:
Grettir's Saga, presented here as The Saga of Grettir the Strong, is credited to an unknown author and described as written in Icelandic sometime in the early fourteenth century. Its opening chapters go back generations before Grettir himself, to his ancestor Onund, son of Ofeig Clumsyfoot.

Onund, brother of Gudbjorg and a kinsman of King Olaf the Saint's line, harried in the West with Balki, Orm the Wealthy and Hallvard, commanding five ships. They attacked King Kjarval in the Barra Isles, captured his ships and much booty, wintered there, and spent three summers harrying Ireland and Scotland. Chapter two turns to Harald Shockhead's bid for supreme kingship in a disturbed Norway and the Battle of Hafrsfjord.
the-story-of-burnt-njal-from-the-iceland: Sir George Webbe Dasent translated this Icelandic saga of Burnt Njal, issued by E. P. Dutton in New York and Grant Richards in London in 1900, with a prefatory note and an introduction abridged from his original edition of 1861. Only the opening pages are present here. They include a transcriber's note on punctuation. They quote Gunnar's famous resolve. He would ride back home rather than fare abroad. A note on the cover design follows. The design joins Gunnar's bill, Skarphedinn's axe, and Kari's sword. The saga itself does not appear.
